      <content name="title">Uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that forms in tissues of the uterus, which is sometimes called the womb. The uterus is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy.</p><p>There are two types of uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>:</p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is the most common type. This type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> begins in the cells lining the uterus, known as the endometrium.</li><li>Uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">sarcoma</span></span> is a rare, more aggressive <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that is harder to treat. This type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> begins in muscle or other tissues in the uterus.</li></ul>Who is more likely to develop uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> usually happens after menopause. The cause is unknown. However, some factors and conditions that change the balance of hormones in your body may increase your risk. These can include obesity or metabolic syndrome (a group of risk factors for certain health problems).</p><p>Other factors and conditions that may increase your risk for:</p><p><span class="qt0">Endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></p><ul><li>Taking estrogen-only hormone therapy after menopause.</li><li>Having type 2 diabetes</li><li>Starting menstruation at an early age or menopause at a later age</li><li>Having never been pregnant</li><li>Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li><li>Having polycystic ovary syndrome</li><li>Having a mother, sister, or daughter who has had <span class="qt0">endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li><li>Having certain genetic conditions, such as Lynch syndrome</li><li>Having <span class="qt0">endometrial</span> hyperplasia (thickening of the uterine lining)</li></ul><p>Uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">sarcoma</span></span></p><ul><li>Having had past treatment with radiation therapy to the pelvis</li><li>Taking tamoxifen, a medicine used to prevent or treat breast <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span></li></ul>What are the symptoms of uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The most common symptom of both <span class="qt0">endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">sarcoma</span></span> is abnormal vaginal bleeding. Both types of uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may also cause pelvic pain or pressure, unusual vaginal discharge, or an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass.</p><p>Less common symptoms may include urinating (peeing) often, having trouble urinating, or pain during sexual intercourse.</p>How is uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>If you have symptoms of uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history and family health history</li><li>Do a pelvic exam</li><li>Order imaging tests</li><li>Suggest a biopsy or a minor procedure called dilation and curettage (D & C) to check the lining of your uterus</li></ul>What are the treatments for uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatment may depend on your health, how much <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> you have, and whether it has spread. The most common treatment is having a hysterectomy, which is surgery to remove the uterus. Sometimes the surgery also removes the ovaries and fallopian tubes.</p><p>You may have more than one type of treatment. Other treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Hormone therapy</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li></ul>Can uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>There is no sure way to prevent uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. But you can do things that may help lower your risk such as aiming for a healthy weight, getting regular physical activity, and talking to your provider about the benefits and risks of hormone therapy.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/polycysticovarysyndrome.html">
      <content name="title">Polycystic Ovary Syndrome</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">PCOS</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Stein-Leventhal Syndrome</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)? <p>Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), also known as polyendocrine metabolic ovary syndrome (PMOS), is the name of a hormonal disorder. PCOS affects the ovaries, as well as many other parts of the body.</p><p>If you have PCOS, you usually have at least two of these problems:</p><ul><li>Not ovulating. Normally, your ovaries make the egg that is released each month as part of a healthy menstrual cycle. This is called ovulation. But with PCOS, the egg may not develop as it should, or it may not be released during ovulation. Your periods may be irregular, or you may not have them at all.</li><li>High levels of androgens. Androgens are hormones that are important for normal male sexual development. Women normally make smaller amounts of androgens. Having higher levels of androgens can cause you to have extra body or facial hair (called hirsutism).</li><li>Growths in one or both ovaries. These growths are often clumps of ovarian follicles that have stopped developing. They may appear as cysts, which are small fluid-filled sacs</li></ul><p>Although it's less common, you may not have growths in your ovaries. You may only have symptoms of PCOS, not ovulate, and have high levels of androgens.</p>What causes polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>The exact cause of PCOS is unknown. Research has shown that different factors may play a role, including:</p><ul><li>Genetics. PCOS tends to run in families.</li><li>Imbalances in androgen levels.</li><li>Insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your body can't use insulin properly. Insulin is a hormone that helps move blood glucose (also called blood sugar) into your cells to give them energy. Insulin resistance can lead to high blood glucose levels.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS often develops as young as age 11 or 12, around the time of your first period. But you can develop it later.</p><p>The symptoms can vary from person to person. Some women have few or even no symptoms. They may not realize they have PCOS until they have trouble getting pregnant. Other women may have more severe symptoms.</p><p>The symptoms of PCOS may include:</p><ul><li>Irregular or missed menstrual periods.</li><li>Too much hair on the face, chest, stomach, or thighs.</li><li>Obesity, weight gain, or trouble losing weight.</li><li>Severe acne which may be hard to treat.</li><li>Oily skin.</li><li>Patches of thickened dark skin (called acanthosis nigricans).</li><li>Infertility. PCOS is one of the most common causes of infertility. But many women with PCOS can still get pregnant.</li></ul>What other health problems are linked to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>PCOS is linked to many other health problems, including:</p><ul><li>Insulin resistance, which can lead to prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.</li><li>Heart disease. Having PCOS increases your risk, and this risk goes up as you age.</li><li>High blood pressure.</li><li>High LDL ("bad") cholesterol and low HDL ("good") cholesterol. This increases your risk of heart disease.</li><li><span class="qt0">Endometrial</span> hyperplasia, a condition in which the lining of your uterus, or womb, becomes too thick. This can increase your risk for <span class="qt0">endometrial</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, also called uterine <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Sleep apnea, a disorder that causes you to repeatedly stop breathing during sleep.</li><li>Depression and anxiety.</li></ul><p>Although there are links between PCOS and these conditions, researchers do not know whether:</p><ul><li>PCOS causes some of these problems</li><li>Some of these problems cause PCOS, OR</li><li>There are other conditions that cause both PCOS and these other health problems</li></ul><p>Not everyone who has PCOS will have all these problems. However, you and your health care provider may want to monitor your health for signs of them, so they can be treated early.</p>How is polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed?<p>There is no specific test for PCOS. To find out if you have PCOS, your provider: </p><ul><li>Will do a physical exam, which will include looking for the physical signs of PCOS.</li><li>Will ask about your medical history and family health history.</li><li>May do a pelvic exam to check for signs of extra male hormones and to see if your ovaries are enlarged or swollen.</li><li>May order a pelvic ultrasound to look for growths on your ovaries and check the thickness of your endometrium (the lining of your uterus, or womb).</li><li>May order blood tests, including tests to check your hormone levels.</li></ul>What are the treatments for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)?<p>Treatments for PCOS can help you manage your symptoms. The treatments may include:</p><ul><li>Lifestyle changes, which can help reduce many symptoms. They can also lower your risk for or help manage related health problems. These changes include:
  <ul><li>Maintaining a healthy weight</li><li>Getting regular physical activity</li><li>Eating healthy foods</li></ul>
</li><li>Medicines:<ul><li>Hormonal birth control, such as pills, shots, and IUDs, can make your period more regular. They may also help remove acne and extra facial and body hair. But it's only an option if you're not currently trying to get pregnant.</li><li>Anti-androgen medicines, which block the effect of androgens. This can help reduce hair loss on your head, the growth of facial and body hair, and acne. Providers do use them to help with these symptoms, but anti-androgen medicines are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat PCOS. These medicines can cause problems during pregnancy. Your provider may have you take them with birth control (to prevent pregnancy).</li><li>Insulin-sensitizing medicines, which are medicines that are used to treat type 2 diabetes. They improve insulin resistance and keep your blood glucose levels steady. They may also lower your androgen levels. They are not approved by the FDA to treat PCOS. But they may help with your symptoms.</li><li>Medicines for acne. These medicines come in pills, creams, or gels.</li></ul></li><li>Treatments for hair removal, such as facial hair removal creams, laser hair removal, and electrolysis.</li><li>Fertility treatments if you are having trouble getting pregnant. They include medicines and procedures such as in vitro fertilization (IVF).</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/biopsy.html">
      <content name="title">Biopsy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A biopsy is a procedure that removes cells or tissue from your body.  A doctor called a pathologist looks at the cells or tissue under a microscope to check for damage or disease. The pathologist may also do other tests on it.</p><p>Biopsies can be done on all parts of the body. In most cases, a biopsy is the only test that can tell for sure if a suspicious area is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.  But biopsies are performed for many other reasons too.</p><p>There are different types of biopsies. A needle biopsy removes tissue with a needle passed through your skin to the site of the problem. Other kinds of biopsies may require surgery.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/uterinediseases.html">
      <content name="title">Uterine Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What are uterine diseases?<p>The uterus, or womb, is the place where a fetus grows during pregnancy. Uterine diseases are conditions that affect the uterus. These diseases can be benign (not <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>) or malignant (cancerous). They may affect your menstrual periods, your ability to get pregnant, or the health of your reproductive organs.</p><p>Some types of uterine diseases include:</p><ul><li>Adenomyosis. Tissue that usually lines the uterus grows on the outside walls.</li><li>Cervicitis. Swelling or inflamed tissue of the cervix. The cervix is the lower part of the uterus.</li><li><span class="qt0">Endometrial</span> hyperplasia. An overgrowth of normal cells inside the uterus.</li><li>Endometriosis. Tissue like the lining of the uterus grows in other places in your body.</li><li>Uterine prolapse. The uterus drops in to the vagina due to weakened pelvic muscles. This can happen after a few vaginal births, menopause, or because of obesity.</li></ul>What causes uterine diseases?<p>Various factors can cause uterine diseases. These can include hormonal imbalances, thyroid problems, fibroids, polyps, <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, infection, or pregnancy.</p>What are the symptoms of uterine diseases?<p>Your symptoms will depend on the type of uterine condition you have. The first sign of a problem with the uterus may be abnormal bleeding. Bleeding could occur between periods, be very heavy, or last much longer than usual. Other symptoms may include bleeding after sex or pelvic pain.</p>How are uterine diseases diagnosed?<p>To find out the cause of your symptoms, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Ask about your symptoms and medical history</li><li>Do a pelvic exam</li><li>Order blood tests or imaging tests</li><li>Do a biopsy</li></ul>What are the treatments for uterine diseases?<p>Treatment depends on the cause. It may include pain medicine, hormone therapy, or surgery. Your provider will work with you to choose the best treatment.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/vaginalbleeding.html">
      <content name="title">Vaginal Bleeding</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Dysfunctional uterine bleeding</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Uterine bleeding</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Menstruation, or a period, is a woman's monthly bleeding. Abnormal vaginal bleeding is different from normal menstrual periods. It could be bleeding that is between periods, is very heavy, or lasts much longer than usual. It also includes bleeding that happens before puberty or after menopause. Causes can include:</p><ul><li>Uterine fibroids or polyps</li><li>Hormone problems</li><li>Hormone pills, such as birth control pills and hormone therapy for menopause</li><li><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> of the cervix, ovaries, uterus or vagina</li><li>Thyroid problems</li></ul><p>Bleeding during pregnancy can have several different causes. It is not always serious, but to be safe you should contact your health care provider right away.</p><p>Pelvic exams, blood tests, imaging tests, and other procedures can help your health care provider diagnose the problem. Treatment depends on the cause. Treatments may include medicines, hormones, and surgery.</p></content>
